A festival of the Hachiman Shrine, originally conducted on the 7th day of the lunar New Year. Participants include one adult parent archer and one adult child archer, two male pages, and two young arrow retrievers. After performing ancient rites, arrows are shot from the stage toward a target in front. This ritual is said to have evolved from the {{ill|lt=hamaya|Q138804|WD=Q138804|lt=hamayumi}} used to ward off evil at the beginning of the year, and is designated an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of the city. ; Otebi Shinji : “Otebi Shinji.” Held on the eve of the 2nd Sunday of July. A purification rite associated with Tomo Gion-gū, preceding the mikoshi procession. Formerly held on the 4th day of the lunar 6th month. During the ritual, sacred fire is lit on a large torch placed at the Zuishin Gate, and this torch is carried to the worship hall over the course of an hour. After the mikoshi is brought out and placed in the worship hall, the torch is paraded through the precincts and town to purify defilement. This ritual is designated an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of the city. === Cultural properties === === Important Cultural Properties (national designation) === * Noh Stage (Structure) – Designated November 14, 1953 (Shōwa 28){{National Cultural Properties Database|102|3147|Nunakuma Shrine Noh Stage}}
[http://www.pref.hiroshima.lg.jp/site/bunkazai/bunkazai-data-102010240.html Nunakuma Shrine Noh Stage] (Hiroshima Prefectural Board of Education).
[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5155.html Nunakuma Shrine Noh Stage] (Fukuyama City website).. === Hiroshima Prefecture–designated cultural properties === * Important Cultural Property (Tangible Cultural Property) ** Torii Gate (Structure) – Early Edo period, built in Kan’ei 2 (1625). Designated February 5, 1957 (Shōwa 32)[http://www.pref.hiroshima.lg.jp/site/bunkazai/bunkazai-data-202010110.html Nunakuma Shrine Torii] (Hiroshima Prefectural Board of Education).
[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5156.html Nunakuma Shrine Torii] (Fukuyama City website).. === Fukuyama City–designated cultural properties === * Important Cultural Property (Tangible Cultural Property) ** Pair of Stone Lanterns (Structure) **: Early Edo period, built in Keian 4 (1651). Designated January 31, 1967 (Shōwa 42)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5143.html Nunakuma Shrine Stone Lanterns] (Fukuyama City website).. ** Noh Masks and Boxes (Crafts) **: All from the Momoyama period and donated by {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsunari|Q8190277|WD=Q8190277}}, the first lord of the Fukuyama Domain. They are said to have originally been prized items of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, received by Katsunari from Tokugawa Hidetada together with the Noh stage. The Okina mask measures 19.39 cm in height and 16.06 cm in width, showing Momoyama-period stylistic features. The mask box is a reused item, decorated with gold maki-e on black lacquer depicting Ming-dynasty Chinese genre scenes. The outer box was made to preserve the mask box; an ink inscription inside the lid indicates it was prepared in {{ill|lt=Eiroku|Q1143341|WD=Q1143341}} 8 ({{ill|lt=1565|Q6634|WD=Q6634}}) by the Nakasuga family, hereditary shrine priests. Designated January 31, 1967 (Shōwa 42)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5228.html Noh Masks and Boxes] (Fukuyama City website).. ** Chigusa-made Kagura Tube (Craft) **: Donated in {{ill|lt=Manji|Q1145295|WD=Q1145295}} 3 ({{ill|lt=1660|Q7001|WD=Q7001}}) by {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|WD=Q10565395}}, the third lord of the Fukuyama Domain, together with the Noh stage. The maker, Chigusa, was a Muromachi-period Noh mask carver. The tube is made of paulownia wood with black lacquer and gold maki-e phoenix designs. Designated January 31, 1967 (Shōwa 42)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5227.html Chigusa-made Kagura Tube] (Fukuyama City website).. * Tangible Folk Cultural Property ** Tomo-no-Tsu Strength Stones – Designated together with 3 stones from Sumiyoshi Shrine. Designated September 22, 2000 (Heisei 12)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5271.html Tomo-no-Tsu Strength Stones] (Fukuyama City website).. * Intangible Folk Cultural Property ** Oyumi Shinji – Designated March 31, 1971 (Shōwa 46)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5264.html Oyumi Shinji] (Fukuyama City website).. ** Otebi Shinji – Designated March 31, 1973 (Shōwa 48)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5265.html Otebi Shinji] (Fukuyama City website).. === Visitor information === '''Address''' * Tomo-chō Ushiroji 1225, {{ill|lt=Fukuyama City|Q661038|WD=Q661038}}, {{ill|lt=Hiroshima Prefecture|Q617375|WD=Q617375}} '''Opening hours''' * 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. '''Access''' * From {{ill|lt=Fukuyama Station|Q800797|WD=Q800797}} on the {{ill|lt=Sanyō Main Line|Q1193436|WD=Q1193436}} or {{ill|lt=Sanyō Shinkansen|Q615964|WD=Q615964}} of {{ill|lt=West Japan Railway Company|Q502125|WD=Q502125}} (JR West), take the {{ill|lt=Tomo Railway|Q11663867|WD=Q11663867|lt=Tomo Railway Bus}} and get off at “Tomo-no-Ura” bus stop (approx. 30 minutes), then walk about 10 minutes. It is a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Shikinaisha|UNKNOWN}}, and under the former {{ill|lt=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|Q712534|WD=Q712534}}, it was ranked as a {{ill|lt=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines#Government shrines|Q712534|WD=Q712534|lt=Kanpei-shōsha}}. Today, it is listed as a {{ill|lt=Beppyo Shrine|Q10898274|WD=Q10898274}} under the {{ill|lt=Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077|WD=Q908077}}. In addition to the name “Tomo Gion-gū,” it is also commonly called “Gion-san” or “Ogion-san.” === Enshrined deities === The shrine enshrines the following two deitiesThe description of the enshrined deities is based on the [http://tomo-gionsan.com/yuisyo.shtml History] (official website).. ; Principal deity :* {{ill|lt=Watatsumi|Q1474187|WD=Q1474187|lt=Ōwatatsumi-no-Mikoto}} – Formerly the enshrined deity of Watasu Shrine. ; Associated deity :* {{ill|lt=Susanoo|Q272993|WD=Q272993|lt=Susanoo-no-Mikoto}} – Formerly the enshrined deity of Tomo Gion-gū. === History === The present Nunakuma Shrine was formed in the {{ill|lt=Meiji period|Q3125096|WD=Q3125096}} by the merger of '''Watasu Shrine''' and '''Tomo Gion-gū''', and was renamed “Nunakuma Shrine” in accordance with the listing in the {{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|WD=Q1342448}} {{ill|lt=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|WD=Q11064932|lt=Register of Deities}}“Place Names of Hiroshima Prefecture,” entry on Nunakuma Shrine.. The shrine maintains that Watasu Shrine was the shrine listed in the Engishiki and that it continues to the present day. The current two enshrined deities ({{ill|lt=Watatsumi|Q1474187|WD=Q1474187|lt=Ōwatatsumi-no-Mikoto}} and {{ill|lt=Susanoo|Q272993|WD=Q272993|lt=Susanoo-no-Mikoto}}) were formerly the deities of the respective shrines prior to the merger[http://tomo-gionsan.com/yuisyo.shtml History] (official website).. === Watasu Shrine === [[File:Nunakuma-jinja Watasu-sha-2.jpg|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Watasu Shrine}}{{small|Former shrine building prior to enshrinement in the main hall.}}]] According to shrine tradition, the founding of Watasu Shrine (now Nunakuma Shrine) dates to Year 2 of Emperor {{ill|lt=Chūai|Q179971|WD=Q179971}}, when {{ill|lt=Empress Jingū|Q232803|WD=Q232803}} prayed for safe sea passage by enshrining Watatsumi-no-Mikoto on a sacred stone at this site while heading westward. Upon her return, she offered a “Izuno Takatomo” (a type of bow accessory; {{ill|lt=Tomo|Q11663860|WD=Q11663860}} refers to one such implement), from which the place name “Tomo” is said to have originated. In the mid-{{ill|lt=Heian period|Q193292|WD=Q193292}}, the {{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|WD=Q1342448}} {{ill|lt=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|WD=Q11064932|lt=Register of Deities}} lists a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Shikinaisha|UNKNOWN}} named “Nunakuma Shrine” in {{ill|lt=Bingo Province|Q1049113|WD=Q1049113}}, {{ill|lt=Numakuma District|Q7069042|WD=Q7069042}}. The reading is given as either “Nunasaki” or “Nunakuma.” Later, the location of this shrine became unknown. In early modern scholarship, it is identified with Watasu Shrine, though whether it was located in Tomo remains unclear. In the early modern period, Watasu Shrine is said to have enshrined Sarutahiko-no-Kami and Funadama-no-Mikoto (also called Funatama-no-Mikoto). It is also said to have originally been located either in Ushiroji-Hiramura or Tomo-no-Sekimachi, and to have been relocated to its present site as a subsidiary shrine of the Gion Shrine during the {{ill|lt=Keichō|Q1328185|WD=Q1328185}} era ({{ill|lt=1596|Q6785|WD=Q6785}}–{{ill|lt=1615|Q6784|WD=Q6784}}). During the {{ill|lt=Meireki|Q1192766|WD=Q1192766}} era ({{ill|lt=1655|Q6975|WD=Q6975}}–{{ill|lt=1658|Q6991|WD=Q6991}}), the shrine buildings were rebuilt by the domain lord {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|WD=Q10565395}}“Gods of Japan” states that Watasu Shrine was originally in Nishi-machi, Tomo, but after being destroyed by fire in Keichō 4 (1599), it was relocated to Asadani in Ushiroji Village, and later moved to the precincts of the Gion Shrine when it was rebuilt in Jōkyō 2 (1674).. === Tomo Gion-gū === According to the shrine, the founding date of Tomo Gion-gū is unknown. It is variously said to have been founded during the {{ill|lt=Tenchō|Q1373138|WD=Q1373138}} era ({{ill|lt=824|Q30353|WD=Q30353}}–{{ill|lt=834|Q30381|WD=Q30381}}) or established by invitation during the {{ill|lt=Hōgen|Q1193898|WD=Q1193898}} era ({{ill|lt=1156|Q19653|WD=Q19653}}–{{ill|lt=1159|Q19659|WD=Q19659}}). The enshrined deity was, as now, {{ill|lt=Susanoo|Q272993|WD=Q272993|lt=Susanoo-no-Mikoto}}. The shrine was originally located in Sekimachi, Tomo, but was destroyed by fire in {{ill|lt=Keichō|Q1328185|WD=Q1328185}} 4 ({{ill|lt=1599|Q6803|WD=Q6803}}) and subsequently relocated to its present site“Gods of Japan,” entry on Nunakuma Shrine.. There is also a theory that this Tomo Gion-gū corresponds to the “{{ill|lt=Ekuma no Kunitsuyashiro||WD=|lt=Ekumi no Kunitsuyashiro}}” mentioned in fragments of the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Bingo Province Fudoki|UNKNOWN}}. The shrine was revered as the tutelary deity of Tomo and received many donations from the lords of the Fukuyama Domain, owning shrine lands as well. === Both shrines from the early modern period onward === The subsequent history of both shrines is as follows: * During the Edo period, Tomo Gion-gū stood at this site, with Watasu Shrine as a subsidiary shrine within its precincts. * In {{ill|lt=Meiji period|Q3125096|WD=Q3125096}} 1 ({{ill|lt=1868|Q7717|WD=Q7717}}), Tomo Gion-gū was renamed “Susanoo Shrine.” * In Meiji 4 ({{ill|lt=1871|Q7746|WD=Q7746}}), this Susanoo Shrine was designated as the Shikinaisha, renamed “Nunakuma Shrine,” and ranked as a {{ill|lt=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines#Government shrines|Q712534|WD=Q712534|lt=Kanpei-shōsha}} under the {{ill|lt=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|Q712534|WD=Q712534}}. * In {{ill|lt=1875|Q7764|WD=Q7764}} (Meiji 8) May, it was revised that Watasu Shrine was the Shikinaisha. * In {{ill|lt=1876|Q7766|WD=Q7766}} (Meiji 9) July, the spirit of Watasu Shrine was enshrined in the main hall, and the Gion deity was moved to an associated position (reversal of principal and subordinate). The Funadama deity of Watasu Shrine was reidentified as Ōwatatsumi-no-Mikoto. === After World War II === * In {{ill|lt=1957|Q5311|WD=Q5311}} (Shōwa 32) May, a main hall relocation ceremony was conducted. Offerings of ritual offerings and sacred food were presented by {{ill|lt=Emperor Shōwa|Q34479|WD=Q34479}}{{Cite book |ja |author=Imperial Household Agency |title=The Shōwa Emperor’s Veritable Records, Vol. 12 |publisher=Tokyo Shoseki |date=2017-03-28 |page=327 |isbn=978-4-487-74412-1}}. === Shrine precincts === [[File:Nunakuma-jinja shaden-2.jpg|thumb|220px|right|{{center|Shrine buildings}}]] [[File:Nunakuma-jinja butai.JPG|thumb|220px|right|{{center|Noh stage (National {{ill|lt=Important Cultural Property|Q1188622|WD=Q1188622}})}}]] The '''stone lanterns''' standing in front of the shrine buildings were donated in {{ill|lt=Keian|Q1146135|WD=Q1146135}} 4 ({{ill|lt=1651|Q6956|WD=Q6956}}) of the {{ill|lt=Edo period|Q184963|WD=Q184963}} by the third lord of the Fukuyama Domain, {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|WD=Q10565395}}. They stand 3.24 meters tall. The large lanterns consist of a hexagonal base, a shaft stone 47.4 cm in diameter, and a middle platform, fire box, roof stone, and finial. As exemplary shrine-front lanterns of the early modern period, they are designated Important Cultural Properties of Fukuyama City. Next to the Hachiman Shrine within the precincts are 20 '''chikara-ishi''' (strength stones). All are made of {{ill|lt=granite|Q41177|WD=Q41177}}, oval in shape, and weigh between 118 and 230 kilograms. Each stone bears an inscription; five with known dates range from {{ill|lt=Tenpō|Q1369045|WD=Q1369045}} 15 ({{ill|lt=1844|Q7633|WD=Q7633}}) to {{ill|lt=Ansei|Q1327259|WD=Q1327259}} 5 ({{ill|lt=1858|Q7684|WD=Q7684}}). As Tomo was a maritime town, these stones are thought to have been offered in strength contests during festivals. Together with three stones at a nearby Sumiyoshi Shrine, they are designated as the “Tomo-no-Tsu Chikara-ishi,” Tangible Folk Cultural Properties of Fukuyama City. One level below the main shrine buildings stands a Momoyama-period '''Noh stage'''. The structure is one bay by one bay, single-roofed, gabled, tsumairi style, with shingle roofing. It is said to have originally been a portable stage within {{ill|lt=Fushimi Castle|Q1196273|WD=Q1196273}}, favored by {{ill|lt=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Q187550|WD=Q187550}}, and later granted by the second shogun {{ill|lt=Tokugawa Hidetada|Q314464|WD=Q314464}} to {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsunari|Q8190277|WD=Q8190277}}, the first lord of the Fukuyama Domain, along with the Fushimi Yagura of Fukuyama Castle. During the {{ill|lt=Manji|Q1145295|WD=Q1145295}} era ({{ill|lt=1658|Q6991|WD=Q6991}}–{{ill|lt=1660|Q7001|WD=Q7001}}), the third lord {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|WD=Q10565395}} donated it to the shrine, and in {{ill|lt=Genbun|Q1145754|WD=Q1145754}} 3 ({{ill|lt=1738|Q6996|WD=Q6996}}) it was converted into the fixed stage seen today. Features of its portable construction remain, with numbered markings on each component, indicating it could be transported even to battlefields. The pine and bamboo painted on the kagami-ita (mirror board) date from the original period. The present bridge and dressing rooms, however, are later additions. Due to its valuable Momoyama-period characteristics, the stage is designated a National Important Cultural Property. The '''second torii gate''' at the lowest level of the precincts was donated in {{ill|lt=Kan’ei|Q1192913|WD=Q1192913}} 2 ({{ill|lt=1625|Q6826|WD=Q6826}}) by Mizuno Katsushige (later the second lord {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsutoshi|Q10565388|WD=Q10565388}}) upon the birth of his eldest son (later the third lord {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|WD=Q10565395}}), praying for his health. Although it is of the common Myōjin torii type, the ends of the kasagi are rounded and upturned, and a torifusuma is added, giving it a distinctive form. The upturned ends resemble the “Hizen torii” style, which may relate to the inscription on the pillars reading “Carpenter: Nakajima Yahyōe of Hizen”. This torii is designated an Important Cultural Property of Hiroshima Prefecture. A festival of the Hachiman Shrine, originally conducted on the 7th day of the lunar New Year. Participants include one adult parent archer and one adult child archer, two male pages, and two young arrow retrievers. After performing ancient rites, arrows are shot from the stage toward a target in front. This ritual is said to have evolved from the {{ill|lt=hamaya|Q138804|WD=Q138804|lt=hamayumi}} used to ward off evil at the beginning of the year, and is designated an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of the city. ; Otebi Shinji : “Otebi Shinji.” Held on the eve of the 2nd Sunday of July. A purification rite associated with Tomo Gion-gū, preceding the mikoshi procession. Formerly held on the 4th day of the lunar 6th month. During the ritual, sacred fire is lit on a large torch placed at the Zuishin Gate, and this torch is carried to the worship hall over the course of an hour. After the mikoshi is brought out and placed in the worship hall, the torch is paraded through the precincts and town to purify defilement. This ritual is designated an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of the city. === Cultural properties === === Important Cultural Properties (national designation) === * Noh Stage (Structure) – Designated November 14, 1953 (Shōwa 28){{National Cultural Properties Database|102|3147|Nunakuma Shrine Noh Stage}}
[http://www.pref.hiroshima.lg.jp/site/bunkazai/bunkazai-data-102010240.html Nunakuma Shrine Noh Stage] (Hiroshima Prefectural Board of Education).
[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5155.html Nunakuma Shrine Noh Stage] (Fukuyama City website).. === Hiroshima Prefecture–designated cultural properties === * Important Cultural Property (Tangible Cultural Property) ** Torii Gate (Structure) – Early Edo period, built in Kan’ei 2 (1625). Designated February 5, 1957 (Shōwa 32)[http://www.pref.hiroshima.lg.jp/site/bunkazai/bunkazai-data-202010110.html Nunakuma Shrine Torii] (Hiroshima Prefectural Board of Education).
[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5156.html Nunakuma Shrine Torii] (Fukuyama City website).. === Fukuyama City–designated cultural properties === * Important Cultural Property (Tangible Cultural Property) ** Pair of Stone Lanterns (Structure) **: Early Edo period, built in Keian 4 (1651). Designated January 31, 1967 (Shōwa 42)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5143.html Nunakuma Shrine Stone Lanterns] (Fukuyama City website).. ** Noh Masks and Boxes (Crafts) **: All from the Momoyama period and donated by {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsunari|Q8190277|WD=Q8190277}}, the first lord of the Fukuyama Domain. They are said to have originally been prized items of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, received by Katsunari from Tokugawa Hidetada together with the Noh stage. The Okina mask measures 19.39 cm in height and 16.06 cm in width, showing Momoyama-period stylistic features. The mask box is a reused item, decorated with gold maki-e on black lacquer depicting Ming-dynasty Chinese genre scenes. The outer box was made to preserve the mask box; an ink inscription inside the lid indicates it was prepared in {{ill|lt=Eiroku|Q1143341|WD=Q1143341}} 8 ({{ill|lt=1565|Q6634|WD=Q6634}}) by the Nakasuga family, hereditary shrine priests. Designated January 31, 1967 (Shōwa 42)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5228.html Noh Masks and Boxes] (Fukuyama City website).. ** Chigusa-made Kagura Tube (Craft) **: Donated in {{ill|lt=Manji|Q1145295|WD=Q1145295}} 3 ({{ill|lt=1660|Q7001|WD=Q7001}}) by {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|WD=Q10565395}}, the third lord of the Fukuyama Domain, together with the Noh stage. The maker, Chigusa, was a Muromachi-period Noh mask carver. The tube is made of paulownia wood with black lacquer and gold maki-e phoenix designs. Designated January 31, 1967 (Shōwa 42)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5227.html Chigusa-made Kagura Tube] (Fukuyama City website).. * Tangible Folk Cultural Property ** Tomo-no-Tsu Strength Stones – Designated together with 3 stones from Sumiyoshi Shrine. Designated September 22, 2000 (Heisei 12)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5271.html Tomo-no-Tsu Strength Stones] (Fukuyama City website).. * Intangible Folk Cultural Property ** Oyumi Shinji – Designated March 31, 1971 (Shōwa 46)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5264.html Oyumi Shinji] (Fukuyama City website).. ** Otebi Shinji – Designated March 31, 1973 (Shōwa 48)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5265.html Otebi Shinji] (Fukuyama City website).. === Visitor information === '''Address''' * Tomo-chō Ushiroji 1225, {{ill|lt=Fukuyama City|Q661038|WD=Q661038}}, {{ill|lt=Hiroshima Prefecture|Q617375|WD=Q617375}} '''Opening hours''' * 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. '''Access''' * From {{ill|lt=Fukuyama Station|Q800797|WD=Q800797}} on the {{ill|lt=Sanyō Main Line|Q1193436|WD=Q1193436}} or {{ill|lt=Sanyō Shinkansen|Q615964|WD=Q615964}} of {{ill|lt=West Japan Railway Company|Q502125|WD=Q502125}} (JR West), take the {{ill|lt=Tomo Railway|Q11663867|WD=Q11663867|lt=Tomo Railway Bus}} and get off at “Tomo-no-Ura” bus stop (approx. 30 minutes), then walk about 10 minutes. It is a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Shikinaisha|1=UNKNOWN}}, and under the former {{ill|lt=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|Q712534|WD=Q712534}}, it was ranked as a {{ill|lt=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines#Government shrines|Q712534|WD=Q712534|lt=Kanpei-shōsha}}. Today, it is listed as a {{ill|lt=Beppyo Shrine|Q10898274|WD=Q10898274}} under the {{ill|lt=Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077|WD=Q908077}}. In addition to the name “Tomo Gion-gū,” it is also commonly called “Gion-san” or “Ogion-san.” === Enshrined deities === The shrine enshrines the following two deitiesThe description of the enshrined deities is based on the [http://tomo-gionsan.com/yuisyo.shtml History] (official website).. ; Principal deity :* {{ill|lt=Watatsumi|Q1474187|WD=Q1474187|lt=Ōwatatsumi-no-Mikoto}} – Formerly the enshrined deity of Watasu Shrine. ; Associated deity :* {{ill|lt=Susanoo|Q272993|WD=Q272993|lt=Susanoo-no-Mikoto}} – Formerly the enshrined deity of Tomo Gion-gū. === History === The present Nunakuma Shrine was formed in the {{ill|lt=Meiji period|Q3125096|WD=Q3125096}} by the merger of '''Watasu Shrine''' and '''Tomo Gion-gū''', and was renamed “Nunakuma Shrine” in accordance with the listing in the {{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|WD=Q1342448}} {{ill|lt=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|WD=Q11064932|lt=Register of Deities}}“Place Names of Hiroshima Prefecture,” entry on Nunakuma Shrine.. The shrine maintains that Watasu Shrine was the shrine listed in the Engishiki and that it continues to the present day. The current two enshrined deities ({{ill|lt=Watatsumi|Q1474187|WD=Q1474187|lt=Ōwatatsumi-no-Mikoto}} and {{ill|lt=Susanoo|Q272993|WD=Q272993|lt=Susanoo-no-Mikoto}}) were formerly the deities of the respective shrines prior to the merger[http://tomo-gionsan.com/yuisyo.shtml History] (official website).. === Watasu Shrine === [[File:Nunakuma-jinja Watasu-sha-2.jpg|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Watasu Shrine}}{{small|Former shrine building prior to enshrinement in the main hall.}}]] According to shrine tradition, the founding of Watasu Shrine (now Nunakuma Shrine) dates to Year 2 of Emperor {{ill|lt=Chūai|Q179971|WD=Q179971}}, when {{ill|lt=Empress Jingū|Q232803|WD=Q232803}} prayed for safe sea passage by enshrining Watatsumi-no-Mikoto on a sacred stone at this site while heading westward. Upon her return, she offered a “Izuno Takatomo” (a type of bow accessory; {{ill|lt=Tomo|Q11663860|WD=Q11663860}} refers to one such implement), from which the place name “Tomo” is said to have originated. In the mid-{{ill|lt=Heian period|Q193292|WD=Q193292}}, the {{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|WD=Q1342448}} {{ill|lt=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|WD=Q11064932|lt=Register of Deities}} lists a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Shikinaisha|1=UNKNOWN}} named “Nunakuma Shrine” in {{ill|lt=Bingo Province|Q1049113|WD=Q1049113}}, {{ill|lt=Numakuma District|Q7069042|WD=Q7069042}}. The reading is given as either “Nunasaki” or “Nunakuma.” Later, the location of this shrine became unknown. In early modern scholarship, it is identified with Watasu Shrine, though whether it was located in Tomo remains unclear. In the early modern period, Watasu Shrine is said to have enshrined Sarutahiko-no-Kami and Funadama-no-Mikoto (also called Funatama-no-Mikoto). It is also said to have originally been located either in Ushiroji-Hiramura or Tomo-no-Sekimachi, and to have been relocated to its present site as a subsidiary shrine of the Gion Shrine during the {{ill|lt=Keichō|Q1328185|WD=Q1328185}} era ({{ill|lt=1596|Q6785|WD=Q6785}}–{{ill|lt=1615|Q6784|WD=Q6784}}). During the {{ill|lt=Meireki|Q1192766|WD=Q1192766}} era ({{ill|lt=1655|Q6975|WD=Q6975}}–{{ill|lt=1658|Q6991|WD=Q6991}}), the shrine buildings were rebuilt by the domain lord {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|WD=Q10565395}}“Gods of Japan” states that Watasu Shrine was originally in Nishi-machi, Tomo, but after being destroyed by fire in Keichō 4 (1599), it was relocated to Asadani in Ushiroji Village, and later moved to the precincts of the Gion Shrine when it was rebuilt in Jōkyō 2 (1674).. === Tomo Gion-gū === According to the shrine, the founding date of Tomo Gion-gū is unknown. It is variously said to have been founded during the {{ill|lt=Tenchō|Q1373138|WD=Q1373138}} era ({{ill|lt=824|Q30353|WD=Q30353}}–{{ill|lt=834|Q30381|WD=Q30381}}) or established by invitation during the {{ill|lt=Hōgen|Q1193898|WD=Q1193898}} era ({{ill|lt=1156|Q19653|WD=Q19653}}–{{ill|lt=1159|Q19659|WD=Q19659}}). The enshrined deity was, as now, {{ill|lt=Susanoo|Q272993|WD=Q272993|lt=Susanoo-no-Mikoto}}. The shrine was originally located in Sekimachi, Tomo, but was destroyed by fire in {{ill|lt=Keichō|Q1328185|WD=Q1328185}} 4 ({{ill|lt=1599|Q6803|WD=Q6803}}) and subsequently relocated to its present site“Gods of Japan,” entry on Nunakuma Shrine.. There is also a theory that this Tomo Gion-gū corresponds to the “{{ill|lt=Ekuma no Kunitsuyashiro||WD=|lt=Ekumi no Kunitsuyashiro}}” mentioned in fragments of the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Bingo Province Fudoki|1=UNKNOWN}}. The shrine was revered as the tutelary deity of Tomo and received many donations from the lords of the Fukuyama Domain, owning shrine lands as well. === Both shrines from the early modern period onward === The subsequent history of both shrines is as follows: * During the Edo period, Tomo Gion-gū stood at this site, with Watasu Shrine as a subsidiary shrine within its precincts. * In {{ill|lt=Meiji period|Q3125096|WD=Q3125096}} 1 ({{ill|lt=1868|Q7717|WD=Q7717}}), Tomo Gion-gū was renamed “Susanoo Shrine.” * In Meiji 4 ({{ill|lt=1871|Q7746|WD=Q7746}}), this Susanoo Shrine was designated as the Shikinaisha, renamed “Nunakuma Shrine,” and ranked as a {{ill|lt=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines#Government shrines|Q712534|WD=Q712534|lt=Kanpei-shōsha}} under the {{ill|lt=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|Q712534|WD=Q712534}}. * In {{ill|lt=1875|Q7764|WD=Q7764}} (Meiji 8) May, it was revised that Watasu Shrine was the Shikinaisha. * In {{ill|lt=1876|Q7766|WD=Q7766}} (Meiji 9) July, the spirit of Watasu Shrine was enshrined in the main hall, and the Gion deity was moved to an associated position (reversal of principal and subordinate). The Funadama deity of Watasu Shrine was reidentified as Ōwatatsumi-no-Mikoto. === After World War II === * In {{ill|lt=1957|Q5311|WD=Q5311}} (Shōwa 32) May, a main hall relocation ceremony was conducted. Offerings of ritual offerings and sacred food were presented by {{ill|lt=Emperor Shōwa|Q34479|WD=Q34479}}{{Cite book |ja |author=Imperial Household Agency |title=The Shōwa Emperor’s Veritable Records, Vol. 12 |publisher=Tokyo Shoseki |date=2017-03-28 |page=327 |isbn=978-4-487-74412-1}}. === Shrine precincts === [[File:Nunakuma-jinja shaden-2.jpg|thumb|220px|right|{{center|Shrine buildings}}]] [[File:Nunakuma-jinja butai.JPG|thumb|220px|right|{{center|Noh stage (National {{ill|lt=Important Cultural Property|Q1188622|WD=Q1188622}})}}]] The '''stone lanterns''' standing in front of the shrine buildings were donated in {{ill|lt=Keian|Q1146135|WD=Q1146135}} 4 ({{ill|lt=1651|Q6956|WD=Q6956}}) of the {{ill|lt=Edo period|Q184963|WD=Q184963}} by the third lord of the Fukuyama Domain, {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|WD=Q10565395}}. They stand 3.24 meters tall. The large lanterns consist of a hexagonal base, a shaft stone 47.4 cm in diameter, and a middle platform, fire box, roof stone, and finial. As exemplary shrine-front lanterns of the early modern period, they are designated Important Cultural Properties of Fukuyama City. Next to the Hachiman Shrine within the precincts are 20 '''chikara-ishi''' (strength stones). All are made of {{ill|lt=granite|Q41177|WD=Q41177}}, oval in shape, and weigh between 118 and 230 kilograms. Each stone bears an inscription; five with known dates range from {{ill|lt=Tenpō|Q1369045|WD=Q1369045}} 15 ({{ill|lt=1844|Q7633|WD=Q7633}}) to {{ill|lt=Ansei|Q1327259|WD=Q1327259}} 5 ({{ill|lt=1858|Q7684|WD=Q7684}}). As Tomo was a maritime town, these stones are thought to have been offered in strength contests during festivals. Together with three stones at a nearby Sumiyoshi Shrine, they are designated as the “Tomo-no-Tsu Chikara-ishi,” Tangible Folk Cultural Properties of Fukuyama City. One level below the main shrine buildings stands a Momoyama-period '''Noh stage'''. The structure is one bay by one bay, single-roofed, gabled, tsumairi style, with shingle roofing. It is said to have originally been a portable stage within {{ill|lt=Fushimi Castle|Q1196273|WD=Q1196273}}, favored by {{ill|lt=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Q187550|WD=Q187550}}, and later granted by the second shogun {{ill|lt=Tokugawa Hidetada|Q314464|WD=Q314464}} to {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsunari|Q8190277|WD=Q8190277}}, the first lord of the Fukuyama Domain, along with the Fushimi Yagura of Fukuyama Castle. During the {{ill|lt=Manji|Q1145295|WD=Q1145295}} era ({{ill|lt=1658|Q6991|WD=Q6991}}–{{ill|lt=1660|Q7001|WD=Q7001}}), the third lord {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|WD=Q10565395}} donated it to the shrine, and in {{ill|lt=Genbun|Q1145754|WD=Q1145754}} 3 ({{ill|lt=1738|Q6996|WD=Q6996}}) it was converted into the fixed stage seen today. Features of its portable construction remain, with numbered markings on each component, indicating it could be transported even to battlefields. The pine and bamboo painted on the kagami-ita (mirror board) date from the original period. The present bridge and dressing rooms, however, are later additions. Due to its valuable Momoyama-period characteristics, the stage is designated a National Important Cultural Property. The '''second torii gate''' at the lowest level of the precincts was donated in {{ill|lt=Kan’ei|Q1192913|WD=Q1192913}} 2 ({{ill|lt=1625|Q6826|WD=Q6826}}) by Mizuno Katsushige (later the second lord {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsutoshi|Q10565388|WD=Q10565388}}) upon the birth of his eldest son (later the third lord {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|WD=Q10565395}}), praying for his health. Although it is of the common Myōjin torii type, the ends of the kasagi are rounded and upturned, and a torifusuma is added, giving it a distinctive form. The upturned ends resemble the “Hizen torii” style, which may relate to the inscription on the pillars reading “Carpenter: Nakajima Yahyōe of Hizen”. This torii is designated an Important Cultural Property of Hiroshima Prefecture. File:Nunakuma-jinja tourou-1.JPG|Stone lantern (right of the main hall; Fukuyama City–designated cultural property) File:Nunakuma-jinja tourou-2.JPG|Stone lantern (left of the main hall; Fukuyama City–designated cultural property) File:Nunakumajinja03s2048.jpg|Strength stones (Fukuyama City–designated cultural property) File:Nunakuma-jinja zuishinmon.JPG|Zuishin Gate File:Nunakuma-jinja ichinotorii-2.jpg|First torii gate File:Nunakuma-jinja otabisho.jpg|Watasu Shrine Otabisho (Tomo-chō Tomo) === Subsidiary and branch shrines === [[File:Nunakumajinja01s2048.jpg|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Precinct shrines}}{{small|From the left: Hachiman Shrine; Kamado Shrine and Sai Shrine; Matsuo Shrine, Inari Shrine, and Jinushi Shrine; Itsukushima Shrine and Ushi-tora Shrine; Watasu Shrine; Gokoku Shrine.}}]] * Hachiman ShrineThe list of subsidiary and branch shrines is based on the {{PDFlink|[http://tomo-gionsan.com/keidai.pdf Precinct Map]}} (official website). * Kamado Shrine and Sai Shrine * Matsuo Shrine, Inari Shrine, and Jinushi Shrine * Itsukushima Shrine and Ushi-tora Shrine * Watasu Shrine – Former shrine building prior to enshrinement in the main shrine. * Gokoku Shrine * Tenman Shrine * Ancestral Spirit Shrine === Festivals === === Annual festivals === * Tsukinami-sai (1st of every month)The annual festival section is based on [http://tomo-gionsan.com/saiji.shtml Festivals] (official website). * Tsukinami-sai (14th of every month) * New Year’s Day Festival (January 1) * Kinen-sai (February 17) * Main Festival (May 2) * Great Purification Rite (June 30) * Summer Festival ** Shinkō-sai (2nd Sunday of July) ** Kankō-sai (3rd Sunday of July) * Autumn Festival (Watasu Shrine Main Festival) (Friday to Sunday before the 3rd Monday of September) * Niiname-sai (November 23) === Special rituals === ; Oyumi Shinji : Held on the 2nd Sunday of February. A festival of the Hachiman Shrine, originally conducted on the 7th day of the lunar New Year. Participants include one adult parent archer and one adult child archer, two male pages, and two young arrow retrievers. After performing ancient rites, arrows are shot from the stage toward a target in front. This ritual is said to have evolved from the {{ill|lt=hamaya|Q138804|WD=Q138804|lt=hamayumi}} used to ward off evil at the beginning of the year, and is designated an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of the city. ; Otebi Shinji : “Otebi Shinji.” Held on the eve of the 2nd Sunday of July. A purification rite associated with Tomo Gion-gū, preceding the mikoshi procession. Formerly held on the 4th day of the lunar 6th month. During the ritual, sacred fire is lit on a large torch placed at the Zuishin Gate, and this torch is carried to the worship hall over the course of an hour. After the mikoshi is brought out and placed in the worship hall, the torch is paraded through the precincts and town to purify defilement. This ritual is designated an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of the city. === Cultural properties === === Important Cultural Properties (national designation) === * Noh Stage (Structure) – Designated November 14, 1953 (Shōwa 28){{National Cultural Properties Database|102|3147|Nunakuma Shrine Noh Stage}}
[http://www.pref.hiroshima.lg.jp/site/bunkazai/bunkazai-data-102010240.html Nunakuma Shrine Noh Stage] (Hiroshima Prefectural Board of Education).
[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5155.html Nunakuma Shrine Noh Stage] (Fukuyama City website).. === Hiroshima Prefecture–designated cultural properties === * Important Cultural Property (Tangible Cultural Property) ** Torii Gate (Structure) – Early Edo period, built in Kan’ei 2 (1625). Designated February 5, 1957 (Shōwa 32)[http://www.pref.hiroshima.lg.jp/site/bunkazai/bunkazai-data-202010110.html Nunakuma Shrine Torii] (Hiroshima Prefectural Board of Education).
[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5156.html Nunakuma Shrine Torii] (Fukuyama City website).. === Fukuyama City–designated cultural properties === * Important Cultural Property (Tangible Cultural Property) ** Pair of Stone Lanterns (Structure) **: Early Edo period, built in Keian 4 (1651). Designated January 31, 1967 (Shōwa 42)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5143.html Nunakuma Shrine Stone Lanterns] (Fukuyama City website).. ** Noh Masks and Boxes (Crafts) **: All from the Momoyama period and donated by {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsunari|Q8190277|WD=Q8190277}}, the first lord of the Fukuyama Domain. They are said to have originally been prized items of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, received by Katsunari from Tokugawa Hidetada together with the Noh stage. The Okina mask measures 19.39 cm in height and 16.06 cm in width, showing Momoyama-period stylistic features. The mask box is a reused item, decorated with gold maki-e on black lacquer depicting Ming-dynasty Chinese genre scenes. The outer box was made to preserve the mask box; an ink inscription inside the lid indicates it was prepared in {{ill|lt=Eiroku|Q1143341|WD=Q1143341}} 8 ({{ill|lt=1565|Q6634|WD=Q6634}}) by the Nakasuga family, hereditary shrine priests. Designated January 31, 1967 (Shōwa 42)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5228.html Noh Masks and Boxes] (Fukuyama City website).. ** Chigusa-made Kagura Tube (Craft) **: Donated in {{ill|lt=Manji|Q1145295|WD=Q1145295}} 3 ({{ill|lt=1660|Q7001|WD=Q7001}}) by {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|WD=Q10565395}}, the third lord of the Fukuyama Domain, together with the Noh stage. The maker, Chigusa, was a Muromachi-period Noh mask carver. The tube is made of paulownia wood with black lacquer and gold maki-e phoenix designs. Designated January 31, 1967 (Shōwa 42)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5227.html Chigusa-made Kagura Tube] (Fukuyama City website).. * Tangible Folk Cultural Property ** Tomo-no-Tsu Strength Stones – Designated together with 3 stones from Sumiyoshi Shrine. Designated September 22, 2000 (Heisei 12)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5271.html Tomo-no-Tsu Strength Stones] (Fukuyama City website).. * Intangible Folk Cultural Property ** Oyumi Shinji – Designated March 31, 1971 (Shōwa 46)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5264.html Oyumi Shinji] (Fukuyama City website).. ** Otebi Shinji – Designated March 31, 1973 (Shōwa 48)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5265.html Otebi Shinji] (Fukuyama City website).. === Visitor information === '''Address''' * Tomo-chō Ushiroji 1225, {{ill|lt=Fukuyama City|Q661038|WD=Q661038}}, {{ill|lt=Hiroshima Prefecture|Q617375|WD=Q617375}} '''Opening hours''' * 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. '''Access''' * From {{ill|lt=Fukuyama Station|Q800797|WD=Q800797}} on the {{ill|lt=Sanyō Main Line|Q1193436|WD=Q1193436}} or {{ill|lt=Sanyō Shinkansen|Q615964|WD=Q615964}} of {{ill|lt=West Japan Railway Company|Q502125|WD=Q502125}} (JR West), take the {{ill|lt=Tomo Railway|Q11663867|WD=Q11663867|lt=Tomo Railway Bus}} and get off at “Tomo-no-Ura” bus stop (approx. 30 minutes), then walk about 10 minutes. '''Nearby sites''' * {{ill|lt=Tomo no Ura|Q8194022|WD=Q8194022}} * {{ill|lt=Ankoku-ji (Fukuyama)|Q2850354|WD=Q2850354|lt=Ankoku-ji}} * {{ill|lt=Fukuzen-ji (Fukuyama)|Q11594397|WD=Q11594397|lt=Fukuzen-ji}} * {{ill|lt=Ōta Family Residence (Fukuyama)|Q11444177|WD=Q11444177|lt=Ōta Family Residence / Tomo Seven Courtiers Landing Site}} * {{ill|lt=Iroha-maru Exhibition Hall|Q11260091|WD=Q11260091}} * {{ill|lt=Tomo no Ura History and Folklore Museum|Q11663862|WD=Q11663862}} * {{ill|lt=Hōsen-ji|Q11555114|WD=Q11555114}} === Related literature === * Motohiko Yasu and Yoshihiko Umeda (eds. & supervisors), *Shinto Dictionary*, Jinja Shinpōsha, 1968, pp. 45–46 * Eiji Shirai and Masanori Toki (eds.), *Shrine Dictionary*, {{ill|lt=Tōdō Shuppan|Q11524645|WD=Q11524645}}, 1979, p. 267 === Notes === {{Help footnotes}} {{reflist|2}} === References === * Shrine history pamphlet * Precinct information boards * *{{ill|lt=Japanese Historical Place Name Encyclopedia|Q17213509|WD=Q17213509}}: Place Names of Hiroshima Prefecture* ({{ill|lt=Heibonsha|Q11482108|WD=Q11482108}}), Fukuyama City, entry on Nunakuma Shrine * “Nunakuma Shrine,” in Ken’ichi Tanigawa (ed.), *Gods of Japan – Shrines and Sacred Places – Vol. 2 Sanyō & Shikoku* ({{ill|lt=Hakusuisha|Q4346470|WD=Q4346470}})) === External links === {{Commonscat}} * {{Official website|name=Nunakuma Shrine}} {{Shinto footer}} {{Authority control}} == Categories == [[Category:Wikidata generated shikinaisha pages|Nunakuma Shrine]][[Category:Shikinaisha|Nunakuma Shrine]][[Category:pages]][[Category:pages]] [[Category:pages]][[Category:pages]] [[Category:Beppyo Shrine]] [[Category:Kokuhei-sha]] [[Category:Shikinaisha in Bingo Province]] [[Category:八坂神社]] [[Category:祇園神社]] [[Category:広島県の神社]] [[Category:備後国の式内社]] [[Category:国幣小社]] [[Category:別表神社]] [[Category:重要文化財 (建造物)]] [[Category:福山市の重要文化財]] [[Category:広島県内の市町村指定有形文化財]] [[Category:江戸時代の建築]] [[Category:鞆の浦]] [[Category:福山市の建築物]]

Otebi Shinji (eve of the 2nd Sunday of July) |Map = {{Location map|Japan Hiroshima|label=Nunakuma Shrine|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=20|float=center|relief=1|width=200|caption=}} {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=10|marker=religious-shinto|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{coord|34|23|10.8|N|133|22|42.1|E}}}} }} [[File:Nunakuma-jinja ninotorii-2.jpg|thumb|220px|right|{{center|Second torii gate (Hiroshima Prefecture–designated cultural property)}}]] '''Nunakuma Shrine''' (ぬなくまじんじゃ) is a {{ill|lt=Shinto shrine|Q845945|WD=Q845945}} located in Tomo-chō Ushiroji, {{ill|lt=Fukuyama City|Q661038|WD=Q661038}}, {{ill|lt=Hiroshima Prefecture|Q617375|WD=Q617375}}. It is a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Shikinaisha|1=UNKNOWN}}, and under the former {{ill|lt=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|Q712534|WD=Q712534}}, it was ranked as a {{ill|lt=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines#Government shrines|Q712534|WD=Q712534|lt=Kanpei-shōsha}}. Today, it is listed as a {{ill|lt=Beppyo Shrine|Q10898274|WD=Q10898274}} under the {{ill|lt=Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077|WD=Q908077}}. In addition to the name “Tomo Gion-gū,” it is also commonly called “Gion-san” or “Ogion-san.” === Enshrined deities === The shrine enshrines the following two deitiesThe description of the enshrined deities is based on the [http://tomo-gionsan.com/yuisyo.shtml History] (official website).. ; Principal deity :* {{ill|lt=Watatsumi|Q1474187|WD=Q1474187|lt=Ōwatatsumi-no-Mikoto}} – Formerly the enshrined deity of Watasu Shrine. ; Associated deity :* {{ill|lt=Susanoo|Q272993|WD=Q272993|lt=Susanoo-no-Mikoto}} – Formerly the enshrined deity of Tomo Gion-gū. === History === The present Nunakuma Shrine was formed in the {{ill|lt=Meiji period|Q3125096|WD=Q3125096}} by the merger of '''Watasu Shrine''' and '''Tomo Gion-gū''', and was renamed “Nunakuma Shrine” in accordance with the listing in the {{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|WD=Q1342448}} {{ill|lt=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|WD=Q11064932|lt=Register of Deities}}“Place Names of Hiroshima Prefecture,” entry on Nunakuma Shrine.. The shrine maintains that Watasu Shrine was the shrine listed in the Engishiki and that it continues to the present day. The current two enshrined deities ({{ill|lt=Watatsumi|Q1474187|WD=Q1474187|lt=Ōwatatsumi-no-Mikoto}} and {{ill|lt=Susanoo|Q272993|WD=Q272993|lt=Susanoo-no-Mikoto}}) were formerly the deities of the respective shrines prior to the merger[http://tomo-gionsan.com/yuisyo.shtml History] (official website).. === Watasu Shrine === [[File:Nunakuma-jinja Watasu-sha-2.jpg|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Watasu Shrine}}{{small|Former shrine building prior to enshrinement in the main hall.}}]] According to shrine tradition, the founding of Watasu Shrine (now Nunakuma Shrine) dates to Year 2 of Emperor {{ill|lt=Chūai|Q179971|WD=Q179971}}, when {{ill|lt=Empress Jingū|Q232803|WD=Q232803}} prayed for safe sea passage by enshrining Watatsumi-no-Mikoto on a sacred stone at this site while heading westward. Upon her return, she offered a “Izuno Takatomo” (a type of bow accessory; {{ill|lt=Tomo|Q11663860|WD=Q11663860}} refers to one such implement), from which the place name “Tomo” is said to have originated. In the mid-{{ill|lt=Heian period|Q193292|WD=Q193292}}, the {{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|WD=Q1342448}} {{ill|lt=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|WD=Q11064932|lt=Register of Deities}} lists a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Shikinaisha|1=UNKNOWN}} named “Nunakuma Shrine” in {{ill|lt=Bingo Province|Q1049113|WD=Q1049113}}, {{ill|lt=Numakuma District|Q7069042|WD=Q7069042}}. The reading is given as either “Nunasaki” or “Nunakuma.” Later, the location of this shrine became unknown. In early modern scholarship, it is identified with Watasu Shrine, though whether it was located in Tomo remains unclear. In the early modern period, Watasu Shrine is said to have enshrined Sarutahiko-no-Kami and Funadama-no-Mikoto (also called Funatama-no-Mikoto). It is also said to have originally been located either in Ushiroji-Hiramura or Tomo-no-Sekimachi, and to have been relocated to its present site as a subsidiary shrine of the Gion Shrine during the {{ill|lt=Keichō|Q1328185|WD=Q1328185}} era ({{ill|lt=1596|Q6785|WD=Q6785}}–{{ill|lt=1615|Q6784|WD=Q6784}}). During the {{ill|lt=Meireki|Q1192766|WD=Q1192766}} era ({{ill|lt=1655|Q6975|WD=Q6975}}–{{ill|lt=1658|Q6991|WD=Q6991}}), the shrine buildings were rebuilt by the domain lord {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|WD=Q10565395}}“Gods of Japan” states that Watasu Shrine was originally in Nishi-machi, Tomo, but after being destroyed by fire in Keichō 4 (1599), it was relocated to Asadani in Ushiroji Village, and later moved to the precincts of the Gion Shrine when it was rebuilt in Jōkyō 2 (1674).. === Tomo Gion-gū === According to the shrine, the founding date of Tomo Gion-gū is unknown. It is variously said to have been founded during the {{ill|lt=Tenchō|Q1373138|WD=Q1373138}} era ({{ill|lt=824|Q30353|WD=Q30353}}–{{ill|lt=834|Q30381|WD=Q30381}}) or established by invitation during the {{ill|lt=Hōgen|Q1193898|WD=Q1193898}} era ({{ill|lt=1156|Q19653|WD=Q19653}}–{{ill|lt=1159|Q19659|WD=Q19659}}). The enshrined deity was, as now, {{ill|lt=Susanoo|Q272993|WD=Q272993|lt=Susanoo-no-Mikoto}}. The shrine was originally located in Sekimachi, Tomo, but was destroyed by fire in {{ill|lt=Keichō|Q1328185|WD=Q1328185}} 4 ({{ill|lt=1599|Q6803|WD=Q6803}}) and subsequently relocated to its present site“Gods of Japan,” entry on Nunakuma Shrine.. There is also a theory that this Tomo Gion-gū corresponds to the “{{ill|lt=Ekuma no Kunitsuyashiro|UNKNOWN|WD=|lt=Ekumi no Kunitsuyashiro}}” mentioned in fragments of the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Bingo Province Fudoki|1=UNKNOWN}}. The shrine was revered as the tutelary deity of Tomo and received many donations from the lords of the Fukuyama Domain, owning shrine lands as well. === Both shrines from the early modern period onward === The subsequent history of both shrines is as follows: * During the Edo period, Tomo Gion-gū stood at this site, with Watasu Shrine as a subsidiary shrine within its precincts. * In {{ill|lt=Meiji period|Q3125096|WD=Q3125096}} 1 ({{ill|lt=1868|Q7717|WD=Q7717}}), Tomo Gion-gū was renamed “Susanoo Shrine.” * In Meiji 4 ({{ill|lt=1871|Q7746|WD=Q7746}}), this Susanoo Shrine was designated as the Shikinaisha, renamed “Nunakuma Shrine,” and ranked as a {{ill|lt=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines#Government shrines|Q712534|WD=Q712534|lt=Kanpei-shōsha}} under the {{ill|lt=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|Q712534|WD=Q712534}}. * In {{ill|lt=1875|Q7764|WD=Q7764}} (Meiji 8) May, it was revised that Watasu Shrine was the Shikinaisha. * In {{ill|lt=1876|Q7766|WD=Q7766}} (Meiji 9) July, the spirit of Watasu Shrine was enshrined in the main hall, and the Gion deity was moved to an associated position (reversal of principal and subordinate). The Funadama deity of Watasu Shrine was reidentified as Ōwatatsumi-no-Mikoto. === After World War II === * In {{ill|lt=1957|Q5311|WD=Q5311}} (Shōwa 32) May, a main hall relocation ceremony was conducted. Offerings of ritual offerings and sacred food were presented by {{ill|lt=Emperor Shōwa|Q34479|WD=Q34479}}{{Cite book |ja |author=Imperial Household Agency |title=The Shōwa Emperor’s Veritable Records, Vol. 12 |publisher=Tokyo Shoseki |date=2017-03-28 |page=327 |isbn=978-4-487-74412-1}}. === Shrine precincts === [[File:Nunakuma-jinja shaden-2.jpg|thumb|220px|right|{{center|Shrine buildings}}]] [[File:Nunakuma-jinja butai.JPG|thumb|220px|right|{{center|Noh stage (National {{ill|lt=Important Cultural Property|Q1188622|WD=Q1188622}})}}]] The '''stone lanterns''' standing in front of the shrine buildings were donated in {{ill|lt=Keian|Q1146135|WD=Q1146135}} 4 ({{ill|lt=1651|Q6956|WD=Q6956}}) of the {{ill|lt=Edo period|Q184963|WD=Q184963}} by the third lord of the Fukuyama Domain, {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|WD=Q10565395}}. They stand 3.24 meters tall. The large lanterns consist of a hexagonal base, a shaft stone 47.4 cm in diameter, and a middle platform, fire box, roof stone, and finial. As exemplary shrine-front lanterns of the early modern period, they are designated Important Cultural Properties of Fukuyama City. Next to the Hachiman Shrine within the precincts are 20 '''chikara-ishi''' (strength stones). All are made of {{ill|lt=granite|Q41177|WD=Q41177}}, oval in shape, and weigh between 118 and 230 kilograms. Each stone bears an inscription; five with known dates range from {{ill|lt=Tenpō|Q1369045|WD=Q1369045}} 15 ({{ill|lt=1844|Q7633|WD=Q7633}}) to {{ill|lt=Ansei|Q1327259|WD=Q1327259}} 5 ({{ill|lt=1858|Q7684|WD=Q7684}}). As Tomo was a maritime town, these stones are thought to have been offered in strength contests during festivals. Together with three stones at a nearby Sumiyoshi Shrine, they are designated as the “Tomo-no-Tsu Chikara-ishi,” Tangible Folk Cultural Properties of Fukuyama City. One level below the main shrine buildings stands a Momoyama-period '''Noh stage'''. The structure is one bay by one bay, single-roofed, gabled, tsumairi style, with shingle roofing. It is said to have originally been a portable stage within {{ill|lt=Fushimi Castle|Q1196273|WD=Q1196273}}, favored by {{ill|lt=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Q187550|WD=Q187550}}, and later granted by the second shogun {{ill|lt=Tokugawa Hidetada|Q314464|WD=Q314464}} to {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsunari|Q8190277|WD=Q8190277}}, the first lord of the Fukuyama Domain, along with the Fushimi Yagura of Fukuyama Castle. During the {{ill|lt=Manji|Q1145295|WD=Q1145295}} era ({{ill|lt=1658|Q6991|WD=Q6991}}–{{ill|lt=1660|Q7001|WD=Q7001}}), the third lord {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|WD=Q10565395}} donated it to the shrine, and in {{ill|lt=Genbun|Q1145754|WD=Q1145754}} 3 ({{ill|lt=1738|Q6996|WD=Q6996}}) it was converted into the fixed stage seen today. Features of its portable construction remain, with numbered markings on each component, indicating it could be transported even to battlefields. The pine and bamboo painted on the kagami-ita (mirror board) date from the original period. The present bridge and dressing rooms, however, are later additions. Due to its valuable Momoyama-period characteristics, the stage is designated a National Important Cultural Property. The '''second torii gate''' at the lowest level of the precincts was donated in {{ill|lt=Kan’ei|Q1192913|WD=Q1192913}} 2 ({{ill|lt=1625|Q6826|WD=Q6826}}) by Mizuno Katsushige (later the second lord {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsutoshi|Q10565388|WD=Q10565388}}) upon the birth of his eldest son (later the third lord {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|WD=Q10565395}}), praying for his health. Although it is of the common Myōjin torii type, the ends of the kasagi are rounded and upturned, and a torifusuma is added, giving it a distinctive form. The upturned ends resemble the “Hizen torii” style, which may relate to the inscription on the pillars reading “Carpenter: Nakajima Yahyōe of Hizen”. This torii is designated an Important Cultural Property of Hiroshima Prefecture. A festival of the Hachiman Shrine, originally conducted on the 7th day of the lunar New Year. Participants include one adult parent archer and one adult child archer, two male pages, and two young arrow retrievers. After performing ancient rites, arrows are shot from the stage toward a target in front. This ritual is said to have evolved from the {{ill|lt=hamaya|Q138804|WD=Q138804|lt=hamayumi}} used to ward off evil at the beginning of the year, and is designated an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of the city. ; Otebi Shinji : “Otebi Shinji.” Held on the eve of the 2nd Sunday of July. A purification rite associated with Tomo Gion-gū, preceding the mikoshi procession. Formerly held on the 4th day of the lunar 6th month. During the ritual, sacred fire is lit on a large torch placed at the Zuishin Gate, and this torch is carried to the worship hall over the course of an hour. After the mikoshi is brought out and placed in the worship hall, the torch is paraded through the precincts and town to purify defilement. This ritual is designated an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of the city. === Cultural properties === === Important Cultural Properties (national designation) === * Noh Stage (Structure) – Designated November 14, 1953 (Shōwa 28){{National Cultural Properties Database|102|3147|Nunakuma Shrine Noh Stage}}
[http://www.pref.hiroshima.lg.jp/site/bunkazai/bunkazai-data-102010240.html Nunakuma Shrine Noh Stage] (Hiroshima Prefectural Board of Education).
[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5155.html Nunakuma Shrine Noh Stage] (Fukuyama City website).. === Hiroshima Prefecture–designated cultural properties === * Important Cultural Property (Tangible Cultural Property) ** Torii Gate (Structure) – Early Edo period, built in Kan’ei 2 (1625). Designated February 5, 1957 (Shōwa 32)[http://www.pref.hiroshima.lg.jp/site/bunkazai/bunkazai-data-202010110.html Nunakuma Shrine Torii] (Hiroshima Prefectural Board of Education).
[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5156.html Nunakuma Shrine Torii] (Fukuyama City website).. === Fukuyama City–designated cultural properties === * Important Cultural Property (Tangible Cultural Property) ** Pair of Stone Lanterns (Structure) **: Early Edo period, built in Keian 4 (1651). Designated January 31, 1967 (Shōwa 42)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5143.html Nunakuma Shrine Stone Lanterns] (Fukuyama City website).. ** Noh Masks and Boxes (Crafts) **: All from the Momoyama period and donated by {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsunari|Q8190277|WD=Q8190277}}, the first lord of the Fukuyama Domain. They are said to have originally been prized items of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, received by Katsunari from Tokugawa Hidetada together with the Noh stage. The Okina mask measures 19.39 cm in height and 16.06 cm in width, showing Momoyama-period stylistic features. The mask box is a reused item, decorated with gold maki-e on black lacquer depicting Ming-dynasty Chinese genre scenes. The outer box was made to preserve the mask box; an ink inscription inside the lid indicates it was prepared in {{ill|lt=Eiroku|Q1143341|WD=Q1143341}} 8 ({{ill|lt=1565|Q6634|WD=Q6634}}) by the Nakasuga family, hereditary shrine priests. Designated January 31, 1967 (Shōwa 42)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5228.html Noh Masks and Boxes] (Fukuyama City website).. ** Chigusa-made Kagura Tube (Craft) **: Donated in {{ill|lt=Manji|Q1145295|WD=Q1145295}} 3 ({{ill|lt=1660|Q7001|WD=Q7001}}) by {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|WD=Q10565395}}, the third lord of the Fukuyama Domain, together with the Noh stage. The maker, Chigusa, was a Muromachi-period Noh mask carver. The tube is made of paulownia wood with black lacquer and gold maki-e phoenix designs. Designated January 31, 1967 (Shōwa 42)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5227.html Chigusa-made Kagura Tube] (Fukuyama City website).. * Tangible Folk Cultural Property ** Tomo-no-Tsu Strength Stones – Designated together with 3 stones from Sumiyoshi Shrine. Designated September 22, 2000 (Heisei 12)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5271.html Tomo-no-Tsu Strength Stones] (Fukuyama City website).. * Intangible Folk Cultural Property ** Oyumi Shinji – Designated March 31, 1971 (Shōwa 46)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5264.html Oyumi Shinji] (Fukuyama City website).. ** Otebi Shinji – Designated March 31, 1973 (Shōwa 48)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5265.html Otebi Shinji] (Fukuyama City website).. === Visitor information === '''Address''' * Tomo-chō Ushiroji 1225, {{ill|lt=Fukuyama City|Q661038|WD=Q661038}}, {{ill|lt=Hiroshima Prefecture|Q617375|WD=Q617375}} '''Opening hours''' * 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. '''Access''' * From {{ill|lt=Fukuyama Station|Q800797|WD=Q800797}} on the {{ill|lt=Sanyō Main Line|Q1193436|WD=Q1193436}} or {{ill|lt=Sanyō Shinkansen|Q615964|WD=Q615964}} of {{ill|lt=West Japan Railway Company|Q502125|WD=Q502125}} (JR West), take the {{ill|lt=Tomo Railway|Q11663867|WD=Q11663867|lt=Tomo Railway Bus}} and get off at “Tomo-no-Ura” bus stop (approx. 30 minutes), then walk about 10 minutes. Otebi Shinji (eve of the 2nd Sunday of July) |Map = {{Location map|Japan Hiroshima|label=Nunakuma Shrine|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=20|float=center|relief=1|width=200|caption=}} {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=10|marker=religious-shinto|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{coord|34|23|10.8|N|133|22|42.1|E}}}} }} [[File:Nunakuma-jinja ninotorii-2.jpg|thumb|220px|right|{{center|Second torii gate (Hiroshima Prefecture–designated cultural property)}}]] '''Nunakuma Shrine''' (ぬなくまじんじゃ) is a {{ill|lt=Shinto shrine|Q845945|WD=Q845945}} located in Tomo-chō Ushiroji, {{ill|lt=Fukuyama City|Q661038|WD=Q661038}}, {{ill|lt=Hiroshima Prefecture|Q617375|WD=Q617375}}. It is a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Shikinaisha|1=UNKNOWN}}, and under the former {{ill|lt=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|Q712534|WD=Q712534}}, it was ranked as a {{ill|lt=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines#Government shrines|Q712534|WD=Q712534|lt=Kanpei-shōsha}}. Today, it is listed as a {{ill|lt=Beppyo Shrine|Q10898274|WD=Q10898274}} under the {{ill|lt=Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077|WD=Q908077}}. In addition to the name “Tomo Gion-gū,” it is also commonly called “Gion-san” or “Ogion-san.” === Enshrined deities === The shrine enshrines the following two deitiesThe description of the enshrined deities is based on the [http://tomo-gionsan.com/yuisyo.shtml History] (official website).. ; Principal deity :* {{ill|lt=Watatsumi|Q1474187|WD=Q1474187|lt=Ōwatatsumi-no-Mikoto}} – Formerly the enshrined deity of Watasu Shrine. ; Associated deity :* {{ill|lt=Susanoo|Q272993|WD=Q272993|lt=Susanoo-no-Mikoto}} – Formerly the enshrined deity of Tomo Gion-gū. === History === The present Nunakuma Shrine was formed in the {{ill|lt=Meiji period|Q3125096|WD=Q3125096}} by the merger of '''Watasu Shrine''' and '''Tomo Gion-gū''', and was renamed “Nunakuma Shrine” in accordance with the listing in the {{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|WD=Q1342448}} {{ill|lt=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|WD=Q11064932|lt=Register of Deities}}“Place Names of Hiroshima Prefecture,” entry on Nunakuma Shrine.. The shrine maintains that Watasu Shrine was the shrine listed in the Engishiki and that it continues to the present day. The current two enshrined deities ({{ill|lt=Watatsumi|Q1474187|WD=Q1474187|lt=Ōwatatsumi-no-Mikoto}} and {{ill|lt=Susanoo|Q272993|WD=Q272993|lt=Susanoo-no-Mikoto}}) were formerly the deities of the respective shrines prior to the merger[http://tomo-gionsan.com/yuisyo.shtml History] (official website).. === Watasu Shrine === [[File:Nunakuma-jinja Watasu-sha-2.jpg|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Watasu Shrine}}{{small|Former shrine building prior to enshrinement in the main hall.}}]] According to shrine tradition, the founding of Watasu Shrine (now Nunakuma Shrine) dates to Year 2 of Emperor {{ill|lt=Chūai|Q179971|WD=Q179971}}, when {{ill|lt=Empress Jingū|Q232803|WD=Q232803}} prayed for safe sea passage by enshrining Watatsumi-no-Mikoto on a sacred stone at this site while heading westward. Upon her return, she offered a “Izuno Takatomo” (a type of bow accessory; {{ill|lt=Tomo|Q11663860|WD=Q11663860}} refers to one such implement), from which the place name “Tomo” is said to have originated. In the mid-{{ill|lt=Heian period|Q193292|WD=Q193292}}, the {{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|WD=Q1342448}} {{ill|lt=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|WD=Q11064932|lt=Register of Deities}} lists a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Shikinaisha|1=UNKNOWN}} named “Nunakuma Shrine” in {{ill|lt=Bingo Province|Q1049113|WD=Q1049113}}, {{ill|lt=Numakuma District|Q7069042|WD=Q7069042}}. The reading is given as either “Nunasaki” or “Nunakuma.” Later, the location of this shrine became unknown. In early modern scholarship, it is identified with Watasu Shrine, though whether it was located in Tomo remains unclear. In the early modern period, Watasu Shrine is said to have enshrined Sarutahiko-no-Kami and Funadama-no-Mikoto (also called Funatama-no-Mikoto). It is also said to have originally been located either in Ushiroji-Hiramura or Tomo-no-Sekimachi, and to have been relocated to its present site as a subsidiary shrine of the Gion Shrine during the {{ill|lt=Keichō|Q1328185|WD=Q1328185}} era ({{ill|lt=1596|Q6785|WD=Q6785}}–{{ill|lt=1615|Q6784|WD=Q6784}}). During the {{ill|lt=Meireki|Q1192766|WD=Q1192766}} era ({{ill|lt=1655|Q6975|WD=Q6975}}–{{ill|lt=1658|Q6991|WD=Q6991}}), the shrine buildings were rebuilt by the domain lord {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|WD=Q10565395}}“Gods of Japan” states that Watasu Shrine was originally in Nishi-machi, Tomo, but after being destroyed by fire in Keichō 4 (1599), it was relocated to Asadani in Ushiroji Village, and later moved to the precincts of the Gion Shrine when it was rebuilt in Jōkyō 2 (1674).. === Tomo Gion-gū === According to the shrine, the founding date of Tomo Gion-gū is unknown. It is variously said to have been founded during the {{ill|lt=Tenchō|Q1373138|WD=Q1373138}} era ({{ill|lt=824|Q30353|WD=Q30353}}–{{ill|lt=834|Q30381|WD=Q30381}}) or established by invitation during the {{ill|lt=Hōgen|Q1193898|WD=Q1193898}} era ({{ill|lt=1156|Q19653|WD=Q19653}}–{{ill|lt=1159|Q19659|WD=Q19659}}). The enshrined deity was, as now, {{ill|lt=Susanoo|Q272993|WD=Q272993|lt=Susanoo-no-Mikoto}}. The shrine was originally located in Sekimachi, Tomo, but was destroyed by fire in {{ill|lt=Keichō|Q1328185|WD=Q1328185}} 4 ({{ill|lt=1599|Q6803|WD=Q6803}}) and subsequently relocated to its present site“Gods of Japan,” entry on Nunakuma Shrine.. There is also a theory that this Tomo Gion-gū corresponds to the “{{ill|lt=Ekuma no Kunitsuyashiro|UNKNOWN|lt=Ekumi no Kunitsuyashiro}}” mentioned in fragments of the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Bingo Province Fudoki|1=UNKNOWN}}. The shrine was revered as the tutelary deity of Tomo and received many donations from the lords of the Fukuyama Domain, owning shrine lands as well. === Both shrines from the early modern period onward === The subsequent history of both shrines is as follows: * During the Edo period, Tomo Gion-gū stood at this site, with Watasu Shrine as a subsidiary shrine within its precincts. * In {{ill|lt=Meiji period|Q3125096|WD=Q3125096}} 1 ({{ill|lt=1868|Q7717|WD=Q7717}}), Tomo Gion-gū was renamed “Susanoo Shrine.” * In Meiji 4 ({{ill|lt=1871|Q7746|WD=Q7746}}), this Susanoo Shrine was designated as the Shikinaisha, renamed “Nunakuma Shrine,” and ranked as a {{ill|lt=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines#Government shrines|Q712534|WD=Q712534|lt=Kanpei-shōsha}} under the {{ill|lt=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|Q712534|WD=Q712534}}. * In {{ill|lt=1875|Q7764|WD=Q7764}} (Meiji 8) May, it was revised that Watasu Shrine was the Shikinaisha. * In {{ill|lt=1876|Q7766|WD=Q7766}} (Meiji 9) July, the spirit of Watasu Shrine was enshrined in the main hall, and the Gion deity was moved to an associated position (reversal of principal and subordinate). The Funadama deity of Watasu Shrine was reidentified as Ōwatatsumi-no-Mikoto. === After World War II === * In {{ill|lt=1957|Q5311|WD=Q5311}} (Shōwa 32) May, a main hall relocation ceremony was conducted. Offerings of ritual offerings and sacred food were presented by {{ill|lt=Emperor Shōwa|Q34479|WD=Q34479}}{{Cite book |ja |author=Imperial Household Agency |title=The Shōwa Emperor’s Veritable Records, Vol. 12 |publisher=Tokyo Shoseki |date=2017-03-28 |page=327 |isbn=978-4-487-74412-1}}. === Shrine precincts === [[File:Nunakuma-jinja shaden-2.jpg|thumb|220px|right|{{center|Shrine buildings}}]] [[File:Nunakuma-jinja butai.JPG|thumb|220px|right|{{center|Noh stage (National {{ill|lt=Important Cultural Property|Q1188622|WD=Q1188622}})}}]] The '''stone lanterns''' standing in front of the shrine buildings were donated in {{ill|lt=Keian|Q1146135|WD=Q1146135}} 4 ({{ill|lt=1651|Q6956|WD=Q6956}}) of the {{ill|lt=Edo period|Q184963|WD=Q184963}} by the third lord of the Fukuyama Domain, {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|WD=Q10565395}}. They stand 3.24 meters tall. The large lanterns consist of a hexagonal base, a shaft stone 47.4 cm in diameter, and a middle platform, fire box, roof stone, and finial. As exemplary shrine-front lanterns of the early modern period, they are designated Important Cultural Properties of Fukuyama City. Next to the Hachiman Shrine within the precincts are 20 '''chikara-ishi''' (strength stones). All are made of {{ill|lt=granite|Q41177|WD=Q41177}}, oval in shape, and weigh between 118 and 230 kilograms. Each stone bears an inscription; five with known dates range from {{ill|lt=Tenpō|Q1369045|WD=Q1369045}} 15 ({{ill|lt=1844|Q7633|WD=Q7633}}) to {{ill|lt=Ansei|Q1327259|WD=Q1327259}} 5 ({{ill|lt=1858|Q7684|WD=Q7684}}). As Tomo was a maritime town, these stones are thought to have been offered in strength contests during festivals. Together with three stones at a nearby Sumiyoshi Shrine, they are designated as the “Tomo-no-Tsu Chikara-ishi,” Tangible Folk Cultural Properties of Fukuyama City. One level below the main shrine buildings stands a Momoyama-period '''Noh stage'''. The structure is one bay by one bay, single-roofed, gabled, tsumairi style, with shingle roofing. It is said to have originally been a portable stage within {{ill|lt=Fushimi Castle|Q1196273|WD=Q1196273}}, favored by {{ill|lt=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Q187550|WD=Q187550}}, and later granted by the second shogun {{ill|lt=Tokugawa Hidetada|Q314464|WD=Q314464}} to {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsunari|Q8190277|WD=Q8190277}}, the first lord of the Fukuyama Domain, along with the Fushimi Yagura of Fukuyama Castle. During the {{ill|lt=Manji|Q1145295|WD=Q1145295}} era ({{ill|lt=1658|Q6991|WD=Q6991}}–{{ill|lt=1660|Q7001|WD=Q7001}}), the third lord {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|WD=Q10565395}} donated it to the shrine, and in {{ill|lt=Genbun|Q1145754|WD=Q1145754}} 3 ({{ill|lt=1738|Q6996|WD=Q6996}}) it was converted into the fixed stage seen today. Features of its portable construction remain, with numbered markings on each component, indicating it could be transported even to battlefields. The pine and bamboo painted on the kagami-ita (mirror board) date from the original period. The present bridge and dressing rooms, however, are later additions. Due to its valuable Momoyama-period characteristics, the stage is designated a National Important Cultural Property. The '''second torii gate''' at the lowest level of the precincts was donated in {{ill|lt=Kan’ei|Q1192913|WD=Q1192913}} 2 ({{ill|lt=1625|Q6826|WD=Q6826}}) by Mizuno Katsushige (later the second lord {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsutoshi|Q10565388|WD=Q10565388}}) upon the birth of his eldest son (later the third lord {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|WD=Q10565395}}), praying for his health. Although it is of the common Myōjin torii type, the ends of the kasagi are rounded and upturned, and a torifusuma is added, giving it a distinctive form. The upturned ends resemble the “Hizen torii” style, which may relate to the inscription on the pillars reading “Carpenter: Nakajima Yahyōe of Hizen”. This torii is designated an Important Cultural Property of Hiroshima Prefecture. A festival of the Hachiman Shrine, originally conducted on the 7th day of the lunar New Year. Participants include one adult parent archer and one adult child archer, two male pages, and two young arrow retrievers. After performing ancient rites, arrows are shot from the stage toward a target in front. This ritual is said to have evolved from the {{ill|lt=hamaya|Q138804|WD=Q138804|lt=hamayumi}} used to ward off evil at the beginning of the year, and is designated an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of the city. ; Otebi Shinji : “Otebi Shinji.” Held on the eve of the 2nd Sunday of July. A purification rite associated with Tomo Gion-gū, preceding the mikoshi procession. Formerly held on the 4th day of the lunar 6th month. During the ritual, sacred fire is lit on a large torch placed at the Zuishin Gate, and this torch is carried to the worship hall over the course of an hour. After the mikoshi is brought out and placed in the worship hall, the torch is paraded through the precincts and town to purify defilement. This ritual is designated an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of the city. === Cultural properties === === Important Cultural Properties (national designation) === * Noh Stage (Structure) – Designated November 14, 1953 (Shōwa 28){{National Cultural Properties Database|102|3147|Nunakuma Shrine Noh Stage}}
[http://www.pref.hiroshima.lg.jp/site/bunkazai/bunkazai-data-102010240.html Nunakuma Shrine Noh Stage] (Hiroshima Prefectural Board of Education).
[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5155.html Nunakuma Shrine Noh Stage] (Fukuyama City website).. === Hiroshima Prefecture–designated cultural properties === * Important Cultural Property (Tangible Cultural Property) ** Torii Gate (Structure) – Early Edo period, built in Kan’ei 2 (1625). Designated February 5, 1957 (Shōwa 32)[http://www.pref.hiroshima.lg.jp/site/bunkazai/bunkazai-data-202010110.html Nunakuma Shrine Torii] (Hiroshima Prefectural Board of Education).
[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5156.html Nunakuma Shrine Torii] (Fukuyama City website).. === Fukuyama City–designated cultural properties === * Important Cultural Property (Tangible Cultural Property) ** Pair of Stone Lanterns (Structure) **: Early Edo period, built in Keian 4 (1651). Designated January 31, 1967 (Shōwa 42)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5143.html Nunakuma Shrine Stone Lanterns] (Fukuyama City website).. ** Noh Masks and Boxes (Crafts) **: All from the Momoyama period and donated by {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsunari|Q8190277|WD=Q8190277}}, the first lord of the Fukuyama Domain. They are said to have originally been prized items of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, received by Katsunari from Tokugawa Hidetada together with the Noh stage. The Okina mask measures 19.39 cm in height and 16.06 cm in width, showing Momoyama-period stylistic features. The mask box is a reused item, decorated with gold maki-e on black lacquer depicting Ming-dynasty Chinese genre scenes. The outer box was made to preserve the mask box; an ink inscription inside the lid indicates it was prepared in {{ill|lt=Eiroku|Q1143341|WD=Q1143341}} 8 ({{ill|lt=1565|Q6634|WD=Q6634}}) by the Nakasuga family, hereditary shrine priests. Designated January 31, 1967 (Shōwa 42)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5228.html Noh Masks and Boxes] (Fukuyama City website).. ** Chigusa-made Kagura Tube (Craft) **: Donated in {{ill|lt=Manji|Q1145295|WD=Q1145295}} 3 ({{ill|lt=1660|Q7001|WD=Q7001}}) by {{ill|lt=Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|WD=Q10565395}}, the third lord of the Fukuyama Domain, together with the Noh stage. The maker, Chigusa, was a Muromachi-period Noh mask carver. The tube is made of paulownia wood with black lacquer and gold maki-e phoenix designs. Designated January 31, 1967 (Shōwa 42)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5227.html Chigusa-made Kagura Tube] (Fukuyama City website).. * Tangible Folk Cultural Property ** Tomo-no-Tsu Strength Stones – Designated together with 3 stones from Sumiyoshi Shrine. Designated September 22, 2000 (Heisei 12)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5271.html Tomo-no-Tsu Strength Stones] (Fukuyama City website).. * Intangible Folk Cultural Property ** Oyumi Shinji – Designated March 31, 1971 (Shōwa 46)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5264.html Oyumi Shinji] (Fukuyama City website).. ** Otebi Shinji – Designated March 31, 1973 (Shōwa 48)[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5265.html Otebi Shinji] (Fukuyama City website).. === Visitor information === '''Address''' * Tomo-chō Ushiroji 1225, {{ill|lt=Fukuyama City|Q661038|WD=Q661038}}, {{ill|lt=Hiroshima Prefecture|Q617375|WD=Q617375}} '''Opening hours''' * 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. '''Access''' * From {{ill|lt=Fukuyama Station|Q800797|WD=Q800797}} on the {{ill|lt=Sanyō Main Line|Q1193436|WD=Q1193436}} or {{ill|lt=Sanyō Shinkansen|Q615964|WD=Q615964}} of {{ill|lt=West Japan Railway Company|Q502125|WD=Q502125}} (JR West), take the {{ill|lt=Tomo Railway|Q11663867|WD=Q11663867|lt=Tomo Railway Bus}} and get off at “Tomo-no-Ura” bus stop (approx. 30 minutes), then walk about 10 minutes.
